utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. It is unfortunate that you have been kept waiting this morning. Apparently there were delays in the transportation of the accused. Mr. Guy-Smith, do I understand that you wish to raise a matter at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour, if I might. And I do apologise for the interruption. My client, Mr. Bala, yesterday not only was concerned about the blindfold issue, which has been taken care of, I understand, today, but also was concerned with the inordinate period of time that it took for him to be transported from the gaol to the Tribunal. It took approximately two hours, as I understood it, yesterday. It took approximately the same amount today. The difficulty is as follows for him: It has been, as the Prosecution has acknowledged, known for some period of time that he does have a heart condition, and he is not a particularly well man. And this morning, he said to me that he was feeling extremely ill and was extremely concerned about his state of health, and also was extremely concerned about the fact that each time that he is taken from the prison or at least in the past two days, it has taken an inordinate period of time. I have made this journey from the Tribunal to the prison myself on bicycle and it has taken me 15 minutes. I appreciate the fact that there are certain security concerns or perhaps there's some traffic jams or other reasons why this is occurring. However, his concern was so severe that he, as a matter of fact, said to me initially that he would prefer for proceedings to continue with his absence, with him being back at the prison so he does not have to undergo the stress that is attendant with these accommodations that he has in travelling here. I asked him just before Your Honours came in whether he felt that way for the very moment and he said that what he would like to do is address the Court with regard to this issue if at all possible, because it's a continuing matter that I think is going to be something of grave concern to him and maybe of grave concern to his health. Once again, I do apologise for raising it from the standpoint of I know that there's a process of the Court expected. However, I thought it of sufficient urgency that I wished to address it immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think it would be not useful at this moment if what you are proposing is that the accused personally should address us on the issue. The issue, though, is of course one of concern, that your client should be in a position where he is able to manage the process of the trial without undue strain on his health. Now, quite obviously, the commencement of the trial itself and the fact that yesterday was an unusually long day will have perhaps particularly have aggravated the pressure of the moment, and it may be that when we settle in to a more regular routine, he will find the matter of being in court for half a day as something that isn't as demanding as he experienced yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. With regard to whether that's the case or not, I do not know, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know, but I think we need, as it were, to monitor it. But more importantly, and although it may sound an echo of earlier words that I've uttered, the question of the order in which the accused are moved here and transported back, and therefore, the time that each spends is something that I think could be very usefully discussed between yourself and the Registrar, who has the ultimate running of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And could I suggest that you might follow that avenue and that, clearly, we are all in the hope that, as matters settle in to a routine, your client may find that the pressure of the occasion is not too great for him. Do, of course, feel free at any moment, where it is of serious concern, to raise the matter directly with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is why I raised it this morning. And I will follow the Court's suggestion. However, seeing the speed with which the order that was ordered yesterday was responded to, I thought that perhaps it might be also a good idea to advise the Trial Chamber of what is occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will not at any time enter into discussion as to the Tribunal's -- the Trial Chamber's jurisdiction to make the order that was made yesterday, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not commenting on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seemed to be a way of perhaps resolving what had become something of an impasse in the complex procedures of dealing with an issue that concerned all accused. And so the Chamber was prepared to act as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I speak on behalf of my client and I'm sure the others, that we appreciate the comments that the Chamber has made with regard to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think a slightly different approach may be appropriate in the case of your client at the present time, as I've indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One would hope that that would work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield, I understand you propose an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases, yes. I want to check, if I may, firstly that a bundle of documents that I indicated yesterday we would use during the opening to refer to has in fact reached everyone. It looks something like this, with an index on the front cover. There are, in fact, 11 documents. These are all documents, save possibly one, that were already before the Tribunal at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We all seem to have them, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, that being the case, may I, on behalf of Mr. Limaj, together with my co-counsel, address you on matters that we hope will be of some assistance in relation to his case. And I would like to begin where the Prosecution concluded last night, because their observations where these: That this Tribunal, or the process of this Tribunal, in a sense is a vehicle or an instrument of reconciliation, essentially through justice. The raison d'etre for, again, the Tribunal and its process has been a means whereby individuals and groups of individuals may come to face certain truths and certain facts. Now, we endorse that approach, namely, that you may regard yourselves as part of that process, of course within the parameters that are set on a statutory basis. But bearing that approach in mind, it does immediately highlight the consideration which I ask you to give to the context for this case, both historical and personal. The context for this particular indictment, because we say when one looks at the context and the background to this case, it will be important and relevant to issues that will arise in the substantive hearing in the days hereafter, and it will become relevant, and is relevant and important, in relation to three particular aspects: Firstly, assessing the nature of the conflict in 1998, how it arose, the nature of the response in the early months by the Kosovar Albanians. Plainly, all of these factors may have a bearing on the nature of armed conflict. And may I say at once: I don't intend, plainly, to reiterate the matters or issues raised in the pre-trial brief at this stage. That's the first matter, assessing the nature of the conflict itself in the context of events that went before. Secondly, the context is important in assessing the alleged actions and course of conduct said to have been pursued by this defendant whom I represent, Fatmir Limaj. In other words, one needs to look at, as a contextual matter, the nature of the man himself, who he is, what he's done, both before and after the events alleged in the indictment. Because these, again, may assist in assessing the truth of the allegations made against him. And thirdly, the way the context, in other words, the events before and, to some extent, after, are highly relevant in relation to function of reconciliation through justice, is assessing some of the evidence that you will hear in the light of those events, in order to ascertain whether it has been in any way tainted or politically inspired. So those are three ways in which the context which I wish to develop this morning becomes, we say, relevant and poignant. Before beginning with the narrative of context, although very obvious, it is easy to overlook, especially when one listens at considerable length and in considerable detail to matters that were outlined yesterday, that this indictment in fact is limited in time. It is, in fact, three months of one year: May to July 1998. And it affects, albeit, of course, any one person being unlawfully affected in the sense of murdered, tortured, or unlawfully abducted, is reprehensible and unforgivable in one sense. However, there are a limited number in relation to this indictment, and the word that was used yesterday essentially measured in tens. So a three month period with alleged victims numbering in the tens, not the hundreds, not the thousands. So having said that had as a precursor, what is the context that I'd ask you to consider relevant to this defendant, Mr. Limaj. And what I want to do, if I may, is run the two alongside in the decade before 1998, in other words, the ten years, roughly, that led up to 1998, both for Kosovo and for Fatmir Limaj. They are intertwined, almost inextricably. And to ask you, in a sense, not necessarily now, but as the case goes on, to, as it were, bear in mind the conditions and the situation of an individual like Fatmir Limaj and his family growing into maturity through this decade. And I start with the year 1989. By that year, as you've heard, Fatmir Limaj, having been born in 1971, was 18. He marries in that year, having been educated locally at an elementary school and a secondary school, and it is in 1989 that he enrols in the faculty of law at Pristina. In one sense an unremarkable, ordinary, straightforward, law-abiding young man. But he is living under the shadow, a very dark shadow that is being cast across the whole of Kosovo by a person whose name is now almost household throughout Europe, namely, the newly elected president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, May the 8th, 1989, the very year Limaj marries and enrols at the faculty of law. And it was again in 1989 that a new Serbian constitution revoked the autonomy of Kosovo and began a legislative programme aimed at discriminating against and eliminating the right almost to exist of Kosovar Albanians, and Limaj, of course, is one of those. One has to pause for a moment to imagine without difficulty what it begins to be like for a person of a group who is being targeted out of existence. To begin to appreciate, plainly, I would submit on his behalf, his responsibility, in a sense, for others during these years, one which we will see throughout the matters that I raise this morning, demonstrates someone who wishes to be inclusive, not exclusive, not wanting to erect a form of apartheid which essentially the Milosevic years began, but worse. The following year, 1990, another important year, his first son was born in that year, but that's the year on which the Kosovo parliament was dissolved, July 5th. That's the year in which further legislation of the kind I've already indicated was laid by the Serbs, the Serb government, a policy which was entitled, ironically, the Programme for the realisation of peace, freedom, equality, democracy, and prosperity in the province of Kosovo. Nothing could have been further from the truth. The complete opposite of those tenets, peace, freedom, equality, democracy, and prosperity, were to be wrought upon the Kosovar Albanians. And I want, if I may, just to give you a description which comes from the Human Rights Watch report. I just quote it. I don't ask for it to be on screen or that you have it, but so that it can be checked, it's page 27. This is how Kosovo was described from 1990 onwards, these very years in which this young man is bringing up or attempting to start a family and bring up his family. Kosovo became a police state, run by Belgrade, a strong Serb military presence, committed ongoing human rights abuses. Police violence, arbitrary detention, and torture were common. Ethnic Albanians were arrested, detained, prosecuted and imprisoned solely on the basis of their ethnicity, political beliefs, or membership of organisations or institutions that were either banned or looked upon with disfavour by the Serbian government. Over the ensuing years in this police state, hundreds of thousands, not tens, of Kosovar Albanians were removed, sacked from government institutions. Particularly, of course, this effect was felt in the most important aspect of any society, namely, education. All Albanian teachers were sacked. Albanian-speaking schools were closed. And this process, which affected every aspect of life, the tentacles of this police state reached every aspect of Kosovar Albanian identity. Its object was clear: To eradicate that identity. And it is estimated by Human Rights Watch that in the seven years after 1990, 350.000 Albanians were dispersed in a diaspora which we say is catastrophic. These are all words used by the Prosecution in another context yesterday. A catastrophe occurred through these years to this community purely because of their ethnicity. And towards the end of this seven-year period, that's 1990 through to 1997, in 1996, page 34 of the Human Rights Watch report, human rights abuses intensified. The police acted with near total impunity. Police abuse generally took three basic forms: Random beatings on the streets and in public places, targeted attacks against politically active Albanians and arbitrary retaliation for attacks by the KLA. I pause. Imagine yourselves in your own home countries, where the parliament has been dissolved, you are occupied essentially by a foreign power, and your very existence is denied. No wonder so many thousand left. And in fact, as you've heard, in 1997, Fatmir Limaj was forced himself to flee. This was, in a sense, ethnic cleansing of the worst kind. This was, to use the words that are sometimes espoused in another context, a widespread and systematic attack on a civilian population. We arrive at the door of the year 1998. And it is in this year, yet again, between May and September - Human Rights Watch page 47 - a further 298.000 Kosovar Albanians are internally displaced. And gradually through this year, the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, otherwise known as FRY, the forces of the Republic of Serbia, and MUP, the acronym occasionally used in connection to them, began a more intensive campaign than the one that we have so far outlined. Whole villages were razed to the ground. There was not only destruction of property but, of course, the destruction of men, women, and children, young and old. Once again, the catastrophe and the horror of what was happening is not to be measured in tens but in hundreds and thousands, in terms of people killed and homes destroyed, well beyond, we say, the incident that you're familiar with, the Jashari massacre at Drenica in February and March, three villages then attacked indiscriminately, 83 dead, 24 of whom are women and children, one pregnant woman shot in the face, four brothers of one family killed, ten members of the Ahmeti family summarily executed. One has no doubt at all that in each of those cases the horror and the catastrophe for them was, again, unforgettable. This is to indicate, clearly, that what you are faced with deciding in this case has to be set against what has happened before, particularly when it is said yesterday, in the context of reconciliation, the Prosecution read out a list of those Serbs who have been indicted. However, the list of Serbs who have been indicted do not stand indicted for the years before the 1st of January, 1999. In other words, the events to which I have referred in a little detail have not been made accountable, and there are those within Serbian authority who plainly have not disciplined anyone, nor has anyone else chosen to take action in relation to what has happened. It is in that context that this young man, with a young family by now through these years, he has three more children in the 1990s, three daughters, one born in 1993, another in 1995, and another in 1999. They're now aged 11, 9, and 5. He has also in these years, despite the oppression and the repression, he has graduated from the university I indicated he had entered in 1989. He graduated in 1995, and in 1996, he began his masters' degree in international relations before he had to depart the country in 1997. But through those years, despite everything, there is no suggestion from any quarter that Fatmir Limaj was, as it were, conducting any kind of campaign of hostility or abuse of any kind towards any other racial group within Kosovo. And so it is in the spring of 1998 that he does return to Kosovo, where he was born, to face the might of a well-equipped, long-standing military presence, by trying to breathe life back into pockets and groups of armed resistance, villagers attempting to fend off the might of the onslaught that I have described to you. He himself this morning, no doubt, with your permission, will wish to say a little about that. Before moving on, may I pose one question in relation to this spring period of 1998 with which this indictment is concerned, May to July. The principal question that has been posed, plainly, is whether Lapusnik was a farm or a camp, whether, in fact, plainly, it was a place of detention, torture, and so forth. We merely pose for your consideration at this stage, given the early nature of what was going on in 1998, when Fatmir Limaj returned, and as you've heard, there has been no issue that he, obviously, went to Lapusnik. And what I am about to pose, the question, is one foreshadowed by the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief, paragraph 39. Given the location of Lapusnik, would anyone choose to place a place of detention for civilians right on the front line, 350 metres from Serb forces, such that if you stand in the farmyard, you can see where the Serb forces were stationed. We would submit to you that it doesn't take a great military brain to work out that that is not where you would put civilians. If you are at the stage of the spring 1998 concerned with, primarily, fending off the Serbian military machine, focusing your attention on that, you are hardly going to be, we suggest, distracted and using up scarce resources dealing with bringing civilians from disparate municipalities, across dangerous roads in dangerous circumstances to a highly vulnerable position just in front of the Serb lines. A different matter if you were dealing with prisoners of war, in other words, soldiers or people who were engaged in combat. You might, for sake of convenience, because you have taken or captured them near the front line; you would not, we suggest, necessarily want to bring civilians to that position. It is a question to be asked in relation to the issues that you face. What I indicated was that I wanted to ask you to consider the context of this short period of time. For these purposes, may I then pass to events after this short period of time, as the post-context aspect of it, in other words, how Fatmir behaved in the years immediately after the war was over. On the 16th of October, 1999, the Party for the Democratic Progress of Kosovo, the PPDK, which was formed yesterday, was formed. He played a role in that. And then, of course, the PDK itself, which grew out of it. He was secretary for public relations. And when the first assembly elections were held in 2001, he became chair of the PDK parliamentary group and was, clearly, a deputy, having been elected democratically. It is clear he played a vital role in the fledgling institutions of transition at that time by advocating an inclusive democracy. And the reason why we raise this is the same as the reason we raise the events before this three-month period, namely, is to assess whether this is the man who would have supervised murder and torture and suddenly have changed into the utmost diplomat, and serious and genuine politician seeking a new union within Kosovo, of course, matters which are yet to be determined in the final status talks next year. Once again, he demonstrated extraordinary responsibility when, of course, he might have done quite the reverse if he had wanted to provoke a different political situation and solution. For these purposes, may I ask you to turn to some, we submit, extremely important documents in relation to the nature of the man with whom you are faced today. If you kindly turn to the bundle that you have, the very first document is a letter sent to the Tribunal by the prime minister of the provisional institution of self-government, as it's headed on page 1 of the bundle. A letter sent on the 13th of March. Now, a number of these documents were provided for the purposes of the Tribunal considering the question of provisional release in this case. However, we pray them in aid now so that you have a picture which may, we say, hang over this Tribunal room as we proceed. The opinion of the prime minister speaking on behalf of the Kosovar government, and I'll only read some paragraphs, but it's all here. On the first page: "Let me assure you that I share the opinion of many local and international colleagues involved in our joint efforts to set the rule of law in Kosovo and that Mr. Limaj's attitude vis-a-vis the ICTY has been exemplary. As the prime minister of Kosovo, I do say it frequently that, aside from all our efforts, his willingness to voluntarily face the trial, non-denial of the Tribunal's authority, and full cooperation with the same, have made the strongest impact to keep the situation calm. It was his attitude that helped the most in this respect. In addition to that, of crucial importance have been his address to the citizens, where without any ambiguity he recognised the authority of the ICTY to prosecute him, his clearly made intention to surrender to the same, as well as an appeal that he made to the citizens, asking them not to protest against charges brought against him by the Tribunal but to recognise the authority of the court and work towards strengthening our institutions and the rule of law." May I pause. There had been a massive demonstration in Pristina and Kosovo of a quarter of a million people, and we say, far from exciting and inciting any form of public disturbance or undermining the fragility of the union that he was attempting, with others, to build up, this is not, we say, the action of a man who really and fundamentally wishes to destroy in the way the indictment alleges against him. The next paragraph reads: "Furthermore, Mr. Limaj, with his attitude, has given the most ethical contribution in setting the pattern of behaviour towards your highly respected authority, which in this region as a whole is frequently contested and brought into question. Yet, when it comes to Kosovo, our determination for a full cooperation with the ICTY is firm and honest and should not be accused with those governments and citizens that don't recognise your authority and search for any possibility to avoid fulfilling obligations vis-a-vis the ICTY. Mr. Limaj's behaviour is by every means an illustration of our determination for full cooperation. "I'd find it important too, to highlight that Mr. Limaj has played the most crucial role in the after-war period in Kosovo. He was the most constructive person as a member of the Assembly, providing a critical link between different political and ethnical groups. For that he was, and still is, widely respected and acknowledged. "At the same time, we shall bear in mind that he has no criminal record of any kind. On the contrary; he is an excellent jurist by education and a former fighter who joined the forces of the Kosovo Liberation Army in pursuit of freedom for all Kosovar citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, religion, or political opinion." Now, lest it be said that, of course, the prime minister may or might say that of one of his own deputies, I would submit, given the nature of his position and the democratic institution that he heads, it is unlikely that he would be saying things just for the sake of it, in the context of Kosovo. The same cannot be said of other jurisdictions, possibly. However, if you turn -- or would be kind enough for turn to the next document, to illustrate the point I make. It isn't just the opinion of fellow Albanians in Kosovo. And the next document, page 4, is a letter dated the 28th of April, 2003, from Daan Everts, who was heading the task force of the OSCE. And that, as you will know, played an extremely important role itself in relation to reconstruction within Kosovo. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Kosovo is perhaps one of the most important international organisations. And this is what he had to say when sending a letter to the Chief Prosecutor: "Although I'm unable to pass any judgement on events taking place in the period during the war, I came to know Mr. Limaj quite well during my nearly three years as head of the OSCE mission in Kosovo right after the conflict, when the international community was engaged in the reconstruction of the region. As an active member of the Kosovo Assembly, subsequently transformed from the democratically elected parliament, Mr. Limaj has always advocated inclusive, conciliatory governance, stressing the importance of compromise and accommodation. He forcefully argued in favour of his party, the PDK, joining the joint interim administrative structure (including Serb participation), which was crucial at the time for achieving broad-based agreement on executive rule by the UN administration. He has also taken a firm stand against ethnic violence and nationalist extremism, inside Kosovo as well as with regard to the near civil war in the neighbouring former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and southern Serbia." In short, we say Mr. Limaj has demonstrated a willingness and a propensity for the very function which was described yesterday by the Prosecution of reconciliation and reconstruction. And over the page, page 5, the letter continues: "In short, during a post-conflict period of intense nationalist and extremist tendencies, I found Mr. Limaj to be a politician who was willing to compromise and work constructively with both the international administration and Kosovo's various ethnic communities." We say the importance of this is that this gentleman plainly would not be easily hoodwinked, would plainly be someone able to assess, carefully, the nature of the man with whom he's dealing, and if he thought for one moment that Mr. Limaj was a maverick, if he thought for one moment that Mr. Limaj was manipulating or whatever, there is no doubt that this letter would not have been written. He is supported by the next document, page 6. This is a testimonial, essentially, by Carolyn McCool, and you will see from her CV, curriculum vitae, which appears at page 8, that she has an extraordinarily impressive background in Canada, with innumerous positions and appointments prior to the ones that she took up in Kosovo. We've included them again so that you can see the quality of the people who are making the assessments, outside Kosovo, of this man inside Kosovo. She says, going back to page 6, in paragraph 2: "In August 1999, I went to Kosovo as the first director of the Mitrovica region of Kosovo for the OSCE mission in Kosovo, otherwise known as OMiK, in which position I remained until December 2000. Subsequently, I was transferred to Pristina as the director of democratisation," and then she indicates where she's practiced before, and that I've already indicated. "I first came to know Fatmir Limaj after moving to Pristina Kosovo in early 2001. As the director of democratisation for OMiK it was necessary that I become acquainted with political leaders. I knew Fatmir Limaj as vice-president of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, commonly known as the PDK." Paragraph 4: "After meeting and speaking with Mr. Limaj on a number of occasions, I formed the opinion that he is one of the most open-minded and progressive of the politicians that I know in Kosovo, of any ethnic community. It appeared to me to be transparent at all times that he is committed to an ethnically inclusive and democratic future in Kosovo, integrated into Europe and with close ties to North America, and is equally committed to establishing a society based on the rule of law in order to ensure that integration. Mr. Limaj was, in my experience, at all times eager to cooperate with the international community in Kosovo, whether this was in respect of political party development, the electoral process, or the central Assembly of Kosovo, to which he was elected in November 2001. "Mr. Limaj is not alone in having impressed me in this way. There are others in his political party and members of other political parties and other ethnic communities, who have also shown that their primary interest is in building a future for Kosovo which is ethnically inclusive, democratic, and mindful of the public interest. But in my view, the community of politicians that can be described in this way is relatively small. It is my considered and very strong opinion that Fatmir Limaj is a member of this relatively small community. "Mr. Limaj is without doubt one of those Kosovar Albanian politicians most prepared to deal with Kosovo Serbs in a responsible, open, and honest manner. Throughout my acquaintance with him in 2001, it became apparent that he was interested in Albanian/Serbian dialogue at a level of principle as opposed to simple rhetoric. At every meeting that I saw him at with Kosovo Serbs, he was able to crystallise points and clarify lines of demarcation in ways that were extremely helpful to the process overall. At what we used to call multi-ethnic dialogue meetings, Mr. Limaj was, in my experience, invariably one of the most productive and honest participants. I do not mean to suggest that he agrees with the perceptions or analysis of Kosovo Serbs. Quite the contrary; his views are almost symmetrically opposed to those of Kosovo Serbs. I mean rather to say that Fatmir Limaj is prepared to deal with those issues as a matter of politics and at a level of principle. For instance, I know from personal experience that he is prepared to meet personally and individually with Kosovo Serbs, and does so in a spirit of non-rhetorical moderation and professionalism." Over the page: "I have never heard Fatmir Limaj voice expressions of hatred for people of different ethnic backgrounds, including Kosovo Serbs, nor have I ever heard him incite anyone to violence against anyone else, again of any ethnic community. In my experience, he has always acted in a very correct and courteous manner towards all people, regardless of their ethnic, religious, political, or national backgrounds." Finally: "My high regard for Fatmir Limaj is apparent. I've considered these comments carefully, due to the significance of the charges which he faces and my high respect for the Tribunal. What I saw here reflects my honest opinion, that Mr. Limaj is one of the most progressive and enlightened politicians working in Kosovo today." Perhaps, if I may add, it is unfortunate that he is not there now and able to participate. Clearly you may think that is the highest testimonial anyone could expect, and we say well merited. And so, again, if there are to be matters that you should consider as the case goes on while you listen to the evidence, it may be that you might wish to reflect upon the nature of this man as described. But it isn't just the nature of the man; it is in fact his actions as well, and his approach to the Tribunal and his approach to the charges. Because may I turn in the very latter stages of the chronology, to what happened. We say it's quite important to see what happened when in fact matters came to a head for him personally. On the 27th of January, 2003, the indictment in this case was confirmed. It was sealed, as we know, until the 17th of February, a Monday. On the 15th of February, a Saturday of that year, Mr. Limaj and others had taken a short break. They had in fact gone to Slovenia. And as you will see in a moment, this was known to some of the authorities, that he had gone, important members of the authorities knew that he had gone, even though, of course, by the 15th an indictment had been confirmed and sealed. On Monday, the 17th, while he's still away, he hears about the fact that there are arrests. But we say what is important here, he doesn't evaporate, he doesn't abscond. Because of course if the Prosecution are correct, he must have known, essentially, having committed, according to them, atrocious, atrocious matters in Lapusnik, that he might be one of those that is being sought. But he doesn't, as I say, disappear. He has time to on the 17th. But at that stage, he doesn't discover that it's an indictment including him, but he does the next day, Tuesday, the 18th. And this is where we come to page 10 in the documents. If you'd kindly turn to that page. There is there a transcript of a telephone call. The importance of this call is twofold. One, it informs him about matters concerning himself; two, the telephone was on a mobile, the telephone call. So in fact, we suggest, in the end, the authorities would not have known where he was unless he had himself made it clear, which he did. And we say what happened thereafter is a direct result of Mr. Limaj's responsibility in this matter. If I may just read portions of the tape-recorded conversation, which was broadcast. This is a Reuters journalist who telephones him at 2.30 and tells him about the announcement in Montenegro, and Limaj says: "No. It's the first time I'm hearing about it. Can you read it for me please." It's read over the phone to him. He's asked, over the page, if he's ever met with The Hague Tribunal investigators. He says no. "Would you surrender to the Hague Tribunal?" "Absolutely." "Would you voluntarily surrender" "Absolutely, yes. If I'm one of the indicted, I'll hand over myself voluntarily, but first I'll fly back to Kosovo to greet with my family and will immediately surrender." We submit all of that is perfectly responsible and reasonable. "You are accused for war crimes. Do you feel guilty?" Limaj: "Absolutely not. I fought of fought for the freedom of my people. I don't languish at all on any indictment and I don't feel guilty at all. I'll go to The Hague to defend Kosovo as I've always done." He is thanked by the journalist. Matters don't reside there. If you turn to the next document, this is another statement by the prime minister of Kosovo, a man we submit of considerable responsibility himself. Approximately one and a half hours later, Limaj is not disappearing into the valleys and mountains of Slovenia, knowing, as he does by then, that he's wanted, if he is a guilty man, as alleged. He is in fact doing the reverse. He's remaining where he is and telephoning the prime minister. And a record of that -- a recollection of it, should I say, is set out in this statement, page 12. On the 18th of February, the prime minister writes: "At about 4.00 p.m., Mr. Limaj telephoned me at my official residence. He informed me that he had just learned of the indictment against him and expressed his readiness to surrender himself voluntarily to the Hague Tribunal. To this end, he requested that he should be enabled to return to Pristina from Slovenia and say goodbye to his family and from there immediately travel to The Hague to voluntarily surrender to the ICTY." Over the page: "I'm also aware that prior to his detention, Mr. Limaj made public statements on the Kosovo broadcast media where he expressed both his readiness and determination to turn himself in voluntarily to the ICTY in The Hague. He additionally expressed regret that he was out of Kosovo at the time the indictment was made public. "Given that the field of security in Kosovo is a reserved power for the special representative of the Secretary-General, in my capacity as prime minister of Kosovo, I asked Mr. Steiner to facilitate the return of Mr. Limaj from Slovenia to Kosovo and his onward travel to The Hague. The meeting between the SRSG, Mr. Steiner and myself and other representatives of the Kosovo government" - and he names them - "took place at Mr. Steiner's office from 5.00 to 6.00 on the 18th." You will begin to see that the events after 2.30 indicate a trail of responsibility by the Kosovo government and by this, we say, responsible politician, Mr. Limaj's response. He was, therefore, we say, in the process of arranging a perfectly proper surrender to the authorities. And it is part of his, we say, approach to this Tribunal and the process throughout that he has, as it were, taken it into his confidence and asked the people of Kosovo to do the same. And as you will see in this letter, page 13, one more paragraph: "The SRSG expressed his readiness to travel to Slovenia himself the following morning, the 19th of February, 2003, on a special plane, and to accompany Mr. Limaj from Slovenia back to Kosovo, from where Mr. Limaj would go on to The Hague." And in a later letter, he indicates, I don't ask you to read it, pages 14 and 15, he confirms that he knew the whereabouts in Slovenia when he spoke to Mr. Steiner, which is why that topic was discussed at 5.00. He remained, that is, Mr. Limaj, at his hotel in Slovenia. It is clear that, in fact, prior to his detention by the Slovenian police who went to the hotel in the end a little later, Mr. Limaj made some other broadcasts which are then to be found at page 17 onwards, and these -- some of these are important in relation to, again, assessing Mr. Limaj and his approach to these charges and to the Tribunal. At page 17, we identified yesterday a rather better transcript of what he said on the 18th to the RTK, the Public Television of Kosovo, sometime before his detention in Kosovo. So it's the sheet 17 and 18 which are slightly better and more expanded version of what is on page 19. So if I may just read this. What he says to the interviewer on the 18th, before detention: "To tell the truth, I am, of course, surprised at such a statement, meaning the indictment, or indictment, but I take it as something which, in the end, is a duty that I must perform. At least this is what the Hague Tribunal, a valued international authority, foresees, and of course I will obey its will or ... This indictment prepared by Ms. Del Ponte. As you say, I have been and still am abroad, but now, having received this information one and a half or two hours ago, I will get ready to travel to Pristina and will surrender voluntarily or will travel to the court in The Hague, so that this indictment can go through the normal procedure as it should. No doubt it's been an accident, but as you see from their statements, it seems that there were many who knew about this thing. This was, as is normal, a secret of KFOR or Ms. Del Ponte, and I can confirm that I did not in any way, not a sign, so confirmation or warning of any such thing, and so I continued to perform my ordinary duties and obligations according to the prearranged schedule. And so by chance I found myself away from Kosovo. My greatest wish would have been to be there when this news was brought to me, but I hope that I will be in Kosovo soon and I would request there's no need for anybody to put on a display of any kind, because I am ready for this kind of thing and I am ready to go voluntarily to The Hague. I say voluntarily because I'm very confident and I'm very proud of all my past and what I've done so far. If you ask me what would I change, I say that if I had to live the life I have lived so far one million times over I would not change it for a single second or by one millimetre. I would do the same things again because I am convinced that what I did was done in the service of my country and my people and that I behaved within all national and international norms. Perhaps the greatest crime that I have committed was when my soldiers and I protected 85.000 civilians, people's lives." If I may just interpose. Those are the civilians who were driven into the mountains. "Perhaps this was the greatest crime, in quotation marks, that I could have committed, in not allowing the Serbian fascist troops to commit genocide in the territories where we were active. So on this basis I am ready to go there and I use this opportunity through your television channel to appeal to all my supporters and all citizens not to make something big out of this. Let them take it quietly, because we must be confident that just as we were able to defend Kosovo in very much worse circumstances, so I will be ready to defend Kosovo and our glorious army, the Kosovo Liberation Army, in the procedure that Ms. Del Ponte has set in motion. In the end, it must be clear to all of us citizens of Kosovo that the process through which Kosovo is passing and to which we are all committed to make Kosovo a state is more important than any individual. So I call on everybody not to harm the political process and to continue to carry forward this process until we achieve our state. The fate of individuals is of minor importance and myself, nothing else. I am continuing to do my duty and I see this as a price for the independence of Kosovo, and if I have to pay this price for the independence of Kosovo, I am ready to do such a thing, seeing as we have also been ready to give our lives for Kosovo." We say that is an impressive broadcast, spoken from the heart, with sincerity. At around the same time, page 20.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel please needs to slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: -- And he says at page 20: "You know there had been indictments from The Hague and we have all the obligations to cooperate with The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. The interpreters are having hard time because you are going so fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: "I'm very encouraged about the statement from Fatmir Limaj that he's made. He recognises the responsibility and he recognises his obligations under The Hague and I would like to tell you that I'm also encouraged that the prime minister came here and has told me and confirmed to me that Fatmir Limaj is ready to present himself here to the authorities. I think this is a good sign. That's a very dignified way how we should deal with our obligations of The Hague. And I'm pleased that we have this behaviour from the institutions." And he says much the same in the next answer on this page 20, that he has recognised his responsibility and dealt with an issue -- this issue in a way which is confirmative with the rule of law. "I am proud for this behaviour and I think that's how we have to deal with this issue, in a dignified way." So it's quite clear, even at this stage, that those who have met and know him are assessing him to be a man of responsibility, to be a person who is willing to uphold the rule of law, not undermine it. And that is echoed, finally, on page 25. The intervening pages are other examples of broadcasts at that time. I don't take up your time with those. They are there to be read, if necessary. What appears on page 25, a broadcast again on the 18th by the officer commanding KFOR, General Mini. And I just read the paragraph relating to Limaj himself: "About Limaj was a different approach. Mr. Limaj didn't show, never showed that he wanted to flee or leave the country. He was free to walk, and so he didn't pose any kind of threat to the safe and security of" -- and then it's inaudible: "So we didn't feel that we have to secure immediately. He was the last priority in terms of risks. That's why we knew very well that he is going abroad for a small trip, and it was -- we were also sure that he was coming back, and that is why we didn't make any big operation on him. But of course, this was -- there was also the decision by the International Tribunal to go immediately with the open indictments instead of the sealed indictments. And so the operation was stopped in the middle. Then the last part is taking another option, which was a good option since the beginning, to have the suspected or the accused to surrender himself and this is the case of Mr. Limaj." And over the page, 26, he again takes the opportunity of the broadcast in the middle of the major paragraph there to thank the institutions of Kosovo that supported this operation. And the reactions of the leaders and the cooperation. "Justice is justice, and international justice is something really serious. So the show, the demonstration, maturity by the institutions is a great success for that kind of democracy." And we do say that the reaction of Limaj himself, as well as the institutions and the other politicians, demonstrated that throughout. On the final pages of this bundle, page 27 is a statement in support of Fatmir Limaj by the Assembly of Kosovo. Page 28, another message of support for Mr. Limaj from the president of the Assembly. And perhaps the most important document is the last one, in the light of the allegations in this case. It's headed "Minority Statement," and it occurred on the 14th of June of 2003. It reads: "We the deputies, which in the Kosovo Assembly represent the Bosniaks, Turks, Romas, Ashkalis and the Egyptians, fully aware of our responsibility, do declare and confirm that Mr. Fatmir Limaj is a deputy and head of the PDK parliamentary group and as a senior official of PDK, was always committed to the democratisation of Kosovar society and for the equal integration of all ethnic groups. Mr. Fatmir Limaj has always strived to establish conditions for free life for all ethnic groups and for all citizens of Kosovo, irrespective of their ethnicity, political allegiance or religious conviction. He contributed in the Kosovo Assembly to the creation of good interhuman, interpartisan, and interethnic relations. A tolerant, trustworthy, and respected atmosphere among parliamentary deputies was also his contribution." And then the various members are listed on the very final page. Once again, if one as it were brackets the observations I'm making in the post-period context, with Carolyn McCool and Daan Everts at one end and the minority report at the other, you'd have in between those two brackets a man of substance, a man with responsibility, and a man who is cognisant at all times of the need to provide unity and harmony and reconciliation. And may I say, finally, this on behalf of Mr. Limaj. You will have seen throughout that that he has great respect for the rule of law, great respect for these institutions that were set up by the United Nations in Kosovo and, of course, for this Tribunal. And, therefore, he comes here carrying that respect with him. But as you may for a moment, if you just, as it were, once again put yourselves into his position. He has, in fact, been incarcerated for 20 months. And the reason I light upon these matters at the end is to ask you, and we are confident in the light of what has happened only yesterday and today, that you will be able to be in a position to overcome and dispel another shadow in his life, this time not from Mr. Milosevic at all, but the shadow of prejudice. And it's, of course, an important principle that justice should be done and be seen to be done. And the problem that he's faced in the months up to now has not only been the denial of liberty and the incarceration for 20 months, but also, of course, a matter hopefully now finally resolved, the indignity and trauma of being brought on every occasion, save today, in blindfolds, with no explanation ever being provided to him as to why this man who has contributed so much should be treated in this way. One would have expected at least the courtesy of an explanation. But you may think the final straw for someone facing respectfully the Tribunal has been in the crucial weeks leading up to this hearing, where he's been kept incommunicado, again, at the beginning with no real explanation and certainly the evidential basis not being provided so it can be tested and certainly as I indicated to you yesterday, we suggest there is and was no reasonable basis for doing it vis-a-vis Mr. Limaj. However, the problem with all of this, and we ask that you - and I'm sure you will - carefully consider, that it may give the impression to some, hopefully obviously not yourselves, that, in a sense, his case is prejudged. Why would he be incarcerated? Why would there be blindfolds? Why would there be incommunicado? Unless, underneath it all, underlying it all, is the serious suggestion, the innuendo almost, well, then he must be guilty of something to attract these strictures and this regime prior to the trial itself. And this is topped by, of course, the enormous prejudice that has been created, surrounded this hearing, both inside the Tribunal and outside the Tribunal, by repeated and continuous allegations of witness intimidation, which of course, as you've heard, is being laid again at the door of Fatmir Limaj. This is repudiated. This is the reason that we, as you know, were asking for some time to consider whether this has any manifest basis at all. We suggest it doesn't. However, in view of your approach yesterday, Mr. Limaj is confident that this prejudice that has arisen inside and outside and that might be by some inferred from the conditions that have been imposed is in fact a matter, to use your own words yesterday, of conjecture and speculation. And we do trust this Tribunal to disregard all of this in the process of analysing and assessing the evidence that is to come before you. Do not, we implore you, allow any of those matters to, as it were, fill any gaps that the Prosecution may find themselves faced with in order to provide explanations. It is a very natural tendency and a very natural risk. But once again, dealing with professional Judges, we are confident that it can be laid to rest. And therefore, in that context, a context of a future in which he now feels he will receive a fair assessment, an impartial assessment by an independent Tribunal, all the factors and features of Article 6 of the European convention. And therefore, it's in that context that I would ask permission perhaps - I see the time. It may be after a break or it may be later - for Mr. Limaj himself to address you on related matters to those to which I have addressed you myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just confirm the indication I gave before the break, that we would prefer, and I think the Tribunal would, to hear Mr. Limaj now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
