utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Limaj, there is now an opportunity for you to address the Chamber. I'm sure your counsel has discussed the matter with you. But you should understand you're under no obligation to address us, but you are free to do so if you wish. And this is now the opportunity. And you may do it while seated and from the position that you're now in, if that's convenient. You may sit down, if that's easier, or stand, whichever you feel -- THE ACCUSED LIMAJ: [Interpretation] I think I'd prefer to sit rather than stand, if that's okay with you, Your Honour. I don't know. Can you hear me? Okay. I would prefer to sit, if that's okay with you, Your Honour. Your Honours, allow me first of all to thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak and to express a few words regarding my case. I have talked, certainly, with my lawyers before I asked for this opportunity to address you. Your Honour, I'd like to say that I've been waiting for this opportunity for 20 months now, to speak to you, to hear my views, to hear my truth. I'll try not to repeat what my Defence lawyer already has said to you. However, I think that, speaking about my personal life, my personal biography, I will throw -- I will shed light also on the general situation that prevailed in my country during the time I grew up and during the time of our activity. Your Honour, I come from a family where my parents had -- or have six children. We are three sisters and three brothers. I'm the eldest son. In my narrow family, apart from my parents, I have lived and had, also my uncle and his wife, who unfortunately God did not bless them with a child, and in a way they treated us, their nephews and nieces, as their own children. I want to tell you that I'm very excited, now that I'm talking to you, but also I want to tell you that in the last month, I have been under pressure, under terrible psychological pressure, which I think has been deliberately done before I appeared to you in this court, in this Chamber. Therefore, I kindly ask you to bear that into consideration. Normally I wouldn't feel so excited, but before being here before you, before this Honourable Tribunal, which is not normal, not a common occasion, I feel very excited indeed, very emotional, given the responsibility that I have, but also because of the respect I have for you. As I said, Your Honours, my father is called Kadri Limaj. My uncle, who is now deceased, may God bless his soul, was called Gani Limaj. As the case is with every Kosovo family, my family is not an exception to the rule, we had an average life because of the very poor economic situation in Kosovo and the difficulties we faced in order to make our daily bread and have normal well-being, I would say, for my family. Our parents, our father, worked for 25 years in the well-known city which has become common knowledge to all the world, to Sarajevo, initially as a worker, as an ordinary worker; then afterwards, when I talk, I think you will remember that we used -- at that time the communist dictatorship -- communist government was in power. He managed to be trained and become a team leader in a construction company in Sarajevo. Apart from his regular job, he did also some private work in order to make extra money for the family, to create us better conditions for us living in Kosovo. During all this time, he took good care of us. It was the uncle, actually, who took real good care of us, who educated us. I want to say that I'm one of the hundreds and thousands of Kosovo children who were not blessed with the fact of having the father when they grew up. I'm saying thousands, hundreds and thousands of Kosovo children, because their parents were obliged to work elsewhere, and it was very rarely that they were present when they were born and be present on their birthdays or traditional celebrations, because of the economic difficulties, because of the need they had to work elsewhere. The same holds true of me. The absence of my father was made up by my uncle, and in a very good way indeed, and I consider him as my second parent. Having a very difficult life, everything my parents did was with the aim of educating us, at offering us the possibilities that they themselves were deprived of, in order for us to lead a better life, in order for us to live with our own families, in order for us to contribute to the family, to the family cycle and to the country. After 25 years, Your Honour, of living in the communist system then the workers who had the right, after working for so long, to have a house, an apartment. And this was also the case with my parents, with my father. He, in 1979, he was given an apartment in Sarajevo. But the great wish to be with his children, with his family, and to spend his whole life with them, my father tried to exchange his apartment in Sarajevo with another in Pristina. But he had another aim in mind in doing so. Having a house or an apartment in Pristina, it would be better for us, it would be easier for us to go to school. And fortunately for us, in 1982, my father managed to exchange that house or apartment and find -- with another in Pristina, and find a job in Pristina. And from 1980 to 1983, he's been working in the Elektroenergija plant in Kosovo in Obilic until he retired at an early age, even though that is an unclear issue in Kosovo, that of retirement. So I wouldn't know how to describe his retirement now. But I know that he gets a pension of 50 or to 100 Euro. It's an early pension. He came to Pristina, as I said, which was a good opportunity for us, his kids, to go to school. I did my elementary school in my -- in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Malisevo, in my hometown, whereas the high school I finished in Pristina, in Kosovo's capital, where I also continued with the higher studies. Now in Pristina, where I resettled, so to say, I never broke off my ties with my native town, Banje, and Malisevo, which was the commune, municipality. Apart from the fact that part of my family was there, there were many ties that linked me with my native place. During my school vacation, I used for work and try to help my family, my uncle, my father, to increase what assets we had there. During the high school, as my Defence lawyer said, in 1988, when I was doing my high school studies, dramatic processes started to unfurl in Kosovo, but at the time I was doing my fourth year in the high school, and normally everything was -- what was happening around us was reflected in us, or had an impact on us. I don't want to go into the details of what happened during 1988, what happened in Belgrade, how events developed. I want to speak from my own point of view how I looked at these things in Kosovo. Following the protest, massive protest of 1988, I mean massive because all the people of Kosovo were involved in them and they wanted to protect their leadership that were threatened to be fired from work, and even to be imprisoned by the Milosevic regime, in a public and very firm way, the people voiced their protest, their opposition to these measures, and expressed their support for their own leaders. For all of us, it was clear that this was but the first step that Milosevic was undertaking to come to the liquidation of that single -- of that autonomy we had won in 1974. And unfortunately, things developed, as we foresaw then. Like all the citizens of Kosovo, I too participated in these protests, and in the developments then, as a young enthusiast. Things became more dramatic in 1989, with murders. Only in March 1989, 24 persons who were trying to protect the constitution then of the socialist Federation -- province of Kosovo were killed. They were high school students. Among them, three were girls. I want to remind you of the case -- when I said three girls, one of them, during those protests, she happened to die in my hands and in the hands of a friend of mine. In 1989 I was but only 18 years old. I had never known that girl before. I had never seen her before. She was shot by a bullet, and I wanted to help her, but she died in our hands, as I said. That girl is from Slatine village, which was part of Pristina municipality, now of Kosovo plain, Fushe Kosove. After Kosovo got its autonomy, things continued to deteriorate. I continued my life, like all the people did in those circumstances. When the time came for me after finishing the high school to enrol in the university, I chose to study law, and it was not by accident that I chose that branch. It was because not only myself - I'm talking in this case about myself - but because the entire Kosovo was surrounded by injustices, injustices that were reflected in every moment of our life and in every individual. Nobody was safe from them. Maybe this is the reason why I decided to study law. In 1990, after the dramatic developments in Belgrade and the beginning of the dissolution of the communist system, not of Yugoslavia but the communist system, because then we have later on we have the dismemberment of Yugoslavia. That was the first step, as was said in one of the congresses of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. The student movement in Kosovo in the 1990s, people appeared -- took to the streets in a broad protest to demand democracy and freedom and the establishment of a democratic and pluralistic system in the country. The democratic spirit and movement which had started with the fall of the Berlin Wall had spread rapidly, like in all former Eastern Europe, also in Kosovo. It had a great impact there and on the developments. The student youths were very enthusiastic at this change. I want to make a difference here, I mean I want to explain the motive prompting the youths in different countries, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary, former Yugoslav Republic, Bulgaria. Their motive was to change the system and to win their rights in a free democracy. For us, the students of Kosovo, the motive was even more important, it was extraordinary. Apart from the fact that we realised that through a democratic system we would have more possibilities and we would be freed from a totalitarian system. We Kosovars thought that through these changes, we would win a freedom we never had. We had a double motive through democratisation of former Yugoslavia, through democratisation of Kosovo, the Kosovars thought this was a possibility for them, that the time had come for them to win our freedom and our rights. That's why it's indescribable, the euphoria, the enthusiasm of that time. Your Honours, I want to mention a fact which for us is interesting to point out. The Communist Party, or the Communist League of Kosovo, was the only one in Europe, in the Eastern Europe, that was destroyed earlier, quicker. And this is thanks to our former communist leaders, the leaders who worked under that communist system. They were the first to give up that political organisation, and this wave of developments was followed by the entire people in Kosovo. And for about two weeks in Kosovo, there was no Communist Party or Communist League of Yugoslavia. I'm talking about 1990. I'd like to suggest to you that -- to remind you that the Communist League of Yugoslavia was destroyed much later, was transformed much later. At this time, departure from the Communist League of Kosovo and its transition into new political organisations, it was at that time that new political movements appeared in 1989, we have the Democratic League of Kosovo formed and then following the dissolution of the Communist League of Kosovo, almost the entire people joined this Democratic League of Kosovo, which was regarded as the movement -- as a popular movement, as a movement that will definitely lead the people towards prosperity as a movement, that would definitely lead Kosovo to express the views of Kosovo people, to voice its concerns, to work for the realisation of the people of Kosovo. In all these popular movements, I would like to point out that in the lead of all these changes, transformations, was the youth of Kosovo. I don't think it's superfluous to tell you that Kosovo is a country with a young population. Over 50 per cent of the people are of a young age. So the role played by the youth in the then developments, and later, is decisive. This enthusiasm and these new developments affected everyone. As I said, the entire people joined the movement, this popular movement, which was led by the most eminent figures of our culture, our most prominent intellectuals, in a word, the elite of the intellectual brain of Kosovo at that time. At that time, there were no other parties in Kosovo, because it did not need, I would say, other parties then; it was but the beginning. In 1991, if I'm right, I began to work with a youth parliament. It was a non-political organisation then. It's like a non-government organisation now, I would say. But it was known by the name non-political organisation, whose duty was to organise, mobilise, the youth of Kosovo into various cultural, sports, humanitarian activities, and other activities. In a word, through that organisation, keep the youth under control in the sense of monitoring their education, their cultural activities. Because you have to bear in mind the fact that we didn't have our own institutions. In 1990 - sorry - change occurred in Kosovo, Your Honour. The Assembly of Kosovo, which in 1989 was obliged to - under pressure, under the pressure of tanks, was threatened with gaol and was surrounded, a building was surrounded - was obliged to sign the constitutional amendments to the constitution of 1974. In 1990, it said -- they said their own word, expressed their own will, by proclaiming declaration of Kosovo. Through this declaration, the Assembly of Kosovo made it clear that all the laws that were approved earlier were abrogated and their regulation of the statute of Kosovo would depend on the resolution of the Kosovo -- of the Yugoslav crisis which had just started. Kosovo is waiting to define its status. Kosovar bodies and citizens were -- would be willing to participate in the solution, in the redefining of the status of the new Yugoslavia if all the peoples were -- that had constituted it were to take part in these developments. And Kosovo was in its legitimate right to be one of the factors that -- one of the main factors that would contribute to that Yugoslavia and that would normally enjoy the rights pertaining to it. After this declaration, there was a reaction, a response. I wouldn't say firm; normal reaction maybe, by Milosevic regime, which closed down all the institutions in Kosovo, beginning from the Assembly to the media. In this case, we had the only one public Albanian language television in Kosovo. It was closed down. Imagine, gentlemen, Your Honours, that all these facts that I'm trying to recount before you, imagine that, say, today here in Holland the police entering the premises of television channel and beat and imprison the staff working there, the journalists, close down the television channel, for no reason at all, without giving them any explanation, just because they think differently. What do you think they would do? How would expect that? After the television and the closing down of the only daily, Rilindja in Kosovo, practically Kosovo was plunged into a total information darkness. These developments made our life even more difficult. But Milosevic did not stop at that. He started the campaign of massive expulsion of people from their jobs, firing them, hundreds and thousands of workers were fired from the public administration to the mines they were working and plants. Factories were closed down. The miners were fired from their mines. In a word, everything that was functioning until that time in Kosovo stopped functioning. Every family that made a living through their work could no longer do that because of Milosevic. This went on, the dismissal from work of all the police staff who were Albanians from the court -- Albanians from the courts, from the hospitals, and finally, from the education system. In 1991, I was a student at the faculty of law. I did two years in the premises of the faculty, in the university premises. I want to tell you one of my experiences. We were going to the auditorium to hear our lectures, without knowing that madness would reach that extent. We were supposed to hear a lecture on the right -- on the law, and we were expecting the professor to begin -- to deliver his speech. I was there among the students eager to hear that lecture by that professor, Professor Osmani. We waited for half an hour and nobody addressed us. Then after half an hour, someone told us that the professor is no longer allowed to enter the premises of the university because he's been fired. After three days, not only the professor, Professor Osmani, but nobody, not even the other professors or the students, were allowed to enter the university of Kosovo. They were expelled, so to say. In such a situation, where practically Milosevic had put two million people out of the law -- I mean had deprived their rights, their rights to live, what could the Albanians do under these circumstances? Did they recall their traditions. They had recourse to their most precious values that have kept us surviving during all our history: That is solidarity, close cooperation, helping each other and surviving. In Kosovo, the phase of survival began. It was also the survival of education, because for a long time the Serbian propaganda, with a kind of jealousy within the framework of educational system in Kosovo and also with ardent will of the Kosovar youth which tried by all means to be educated and receive this education, because our parents, they had no such possibility in the past, and also the youth saw the danger in the intellectual brain, or the schools in Kosovo. As I said, during this time of survival of education, this came at foreground and expressing gratitude to all those professors and activists who found ways and means to get organised, and above all, thousands and thousands of professors of schools, of elementary schools, high schools, that I'd like to mention here. I'd like to mention the late -- my former professor and first rector of the university of Pristina, the first rector I'm talking about the years after the 1990s, under the new condition, Professor Doctor Jup Statovci who was at the lead among -- also together with other professors and organised our student lives under new circumstances. We started to hold lectures in private premises, private buildings. The citizens emptied their flats and their houses, their rooms, to offer us the possibility to get education under such circumstances. You cannot imagine how difficult, how difficult it was, what conditions we were learning in and can you imagine that how much education you would have gotten under such circumstances. Thanks to the financing on the part of the people themselves and the all-round help, the readiness and sacrifices of our professors who, with no reward at all, managed to keep the education alive, and at the same time, the indisputable will of the youth to get education, we managed to survive. Not to go long into detail of the problems we faced during the time of our studies, I'd just like to mention one example in 1992. When we started our studies in private premises, me and some friends of mine had to hide the indexes in the building of the school we were learning, we were having classes. In the yard of that house, we had put a place where we had to hide the documents, and from that place we had to go to our flats. So that when the police searched us, they could not be able to find the documents. Because in 1992 and 1993, if they would find such documents with us, it was equal as in, let's say, as in the year 1998. They would say: You're a member of the UCK. There's been hundreds of cases of students were imprisoned and beaten by the police. As I mentioned, the face of survival at that time under this euphoria of course in the eastern Europe, this was just an illusion and there were illusions for a people, and under the circumstances which we lived, they were not strange at all. All of us thought that Europe would get united in 1992, and after 1992, and we would have no problems at all. Each of us would have their own rights. We all thought like this. We all hoped so. Because our eyes were directed towards Europe, toward the West. But that for us was just an illusion, seeing it from the perspective of today, it was just an illusion but that was what it was yesterday and we worked and acted and lived with that kind of logic. However, illusions slowly passed and then we tried to realise, to see the reality we were facing. You see, after all these events in Kosovo, Kosovo fell into an economic and social collapse, under stress, under an entire stress. People were unemployed. They tried to survive. And they were trying to find ways and means how to keep and support their families, because they were like 500.000 people who were dismissed from their work. There were over a million families who practically had no income except for someone who had probably a kind of a small property or a kind of a piece of land in a village. Many of our intellectuals returned to plough their land just to survive. There was another way out of this: To migrate. I mentioned figures of expulsion here, because it was uncontrolled and it was very difficult to know how many people fled Kosovo during -- from the 1990s and onward. During the time when we were attending classes, dozens and dozens of buses from various agencies were transporting, carrying Albanians to the West. And this is a well-known fact to you, I guess. From various countries, say Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, the road they know which way to go and they're paying lots of money and they sold their property. They sold everything they had in Kosovo just for the simple fact of leaving, fleeing the country, and have a kind of a perspective for themselves in the promised West. I'd like to mention here only three occasions which I will never forget them. One morning we were going to the school premises. Always I'm talking about private premises; you know that. We were going to a place where people were waiting for the buses, and the buses were leaving Kosovo in the morning. It was about 100 to 120 buses in the morning. They were filled with people. And this was in front of the Serb authorities. And they knew what was happening, whether they had documents, they had no documents, they were seeing clearly that it was a trade with people. It was an extraordinary smuggling that was taking place. In front of a bus, I saw two old people, woman, an old woman and an old man. And they were yelling. The woman was yelling at something that scared the hell out of us. One in one of my colleagues approached the old woman and was asking why is she crying? What was wrong with her? Was she -- she had bad health or what happened to her? And she said: "I just saw off my son, my only son. He was going abroad to migrate. We were just left, two of us left, two old people." And the old man had his niece -- carrying his niece in his hands and was kissing her just as a grandfather can kiss his niece. And it was difficult to see that scene of parting. And that time, according to the words of the old woman, I understood that the old man was blind. And the little girl was, let's say, his eyes, his eye. It was -- she was his hope. In other words, the little niece led the old man, the blind man, through his life, and it was the time when, because of the economic situation, they had to part. And the two old people were left out in the streets because their son had sold out the entire property to make money and give it to the smugglers or dealers, whatever you can call them, such people. I'd like to mention another occasion here, because there are thousands of such cases that we have seen. But there's such a case that left an impression on me. A traditional family. I'd like to remind you that we Albanians, we have many -- Albanian families have many children. A family that had seven children. The parents were about, say, 45 to 50 years old. However, this family had taken a road of migration because they had not enough money to pay for their trip, and so they were obliged to leave three of their kids in Kosovo, because of the lack of money to pay for the trip. It's unbelievable to see the scene and the horror when you see the mother parting with her own child, because she was unable -- they were unable to travel together or because they were unable to stay together. And when a child -- it's impossible for a child to get away from the mother's bosom. It is hard to see that kind of scene. I mentioned all these just so that you feel, even a little, to feel with the soul of these people, not with papers, not with reports. It is easy to read. It is easy to say good words very easily. You can accuse someone easily. You can prepare for months to say certain words or to say your report, but it is good to experience something. It is very important to see what happened, in fact, not only in a telegraphical way, just to say so. To tell you the truth, during the whole time I had the same danger and inner fear: Will it happen -- will the same thing happen to me, just like many of others? Probably this was a fate that we all had to share. Practically, Your Honours, I did not accept the way of migration because of the family that I had experienced and also for the other fact that I wanted to build my life in my own country. And the moment, the time had come that we had the right to live our life in our country the way we want to live it. And those things I could have avoided I'd like to put them to the service of my country. After graduating the faculty of law in 1994, 1995, I also, so to say, took the road of migration. However, to tell you the truth, my road to migration had another goal: I wanted to continue my studies in Germany. But because the diploma of the faculty of the university that I had graduated from was not recognised, then I had to return or to start my -- to resume my studies from the very beginning. So there were no possibilities for me to resume my studies from the beginning. So I worked in Germany for six months, physical labour, with my own sweat, so that when I returned to Kosovo I had some financial means, resources, to live in Kosovo. I belong to a middle-class family with an average economic level. I had no problems of survival, as I mentioned, compared to what the others had. Fortunately, my parents had some, enough property to lead a normal life, an average life in Kosovo. Because you can imagine what was the demands to lead a normal life in Kosovo at that time. Your Honours, from that part of my biography or background, I'd like to give you a fact that has not been mentioned so far, or probably is not known to you. It seems that it is not known to you or I haven't seen anyone mention it. In 1991, I was a soldier in the Yugoslav army, and I responded to the summon to join the army. Can you imagine after what happened, after all the events that happened in the 1990s, after what happened in Kosovo in 1990, in June 1991, I responded to the summon of the army to continue my military service. After two weeks, conflict broke up in Slovenia, and after Slovenia, right away in Croatia. I was in Bjelovar. It was a small town in Croatia. And the barracks where we served were under the protection or the control of a town called Pakrac. It was one of the first centres where the conflict started between the Yugoslav army and the Croats. After the conflict erupted there, just as many others, I left the army right away, because I was not willing to take part in such a war, neither on the part of the Yugoslavs, which were under the Yugoslav army, no under the part of the Croats, because -- and I returned to Kosovo and continued my life there. After all that I mentioned here, Your Honours, under such a situation, after I returned from Germany, after graduating from the faculty, lack of some future prospects, not to talk about the systematic violence and terror, we -- if we see that from 1990 on, there are hundreds and thousands of our girls who were raped by the police. I'm talking about before, the beginning of the open war. Killings, rapes, beatings, maltreatment. Over 500.000 Albanians from 1990 until 1997 were maltreated, were imprisoned by the Serbian police. No family in Kosovo was -- every family -- there was no family in Kosovo that had not a person of his family without being maltreated by the police. It is a people that were, therefore, kept out of law, or outlawed, we might say so. Under such circumstances, there arises the question. I was at the time 25 years old. If I might ask you all: What do you think? Do you think a 25-year-old man with what I said was prepared to be a lawyer, to serve his own country, to work, find a job, live with his family? Do you think that such a person would choose the road of war or the road of death? I hope not. I don't think that there is anyone with a sound logic that would have made another solution if he had the choice to do so. In the absence of this, Your Honours, we were -- everything was imposed on us. We had our backs against the wall. Every prospect for a better life was missing, was not there. It was a massive humiliation that was done to the compatriots in every step, to your families, to your friends, to your neighbour. You would see humiliation in every step. And there came a moment when it was difficult to cope with such a situation. I just want to mention another fact. You come from a country where I don't know how many migrants from Kosovo live in your countries but I know that in your countries there are many emigrants from Kosovo. And you know quite well that, unfortunately, a part of them have found it impossible to get integrated into your societies. The Albanian emigrants, the Kosovars, until -- there has been Albanian Kosovar emigrants in your countries until 1989. They were known as -- well, known as workers, people who work, mind their own affairs, behave quite well, and hard-working people. Developments after 1990s and the flow of the displacement that I mentioned before toward the West had its own consequences. The overwhelming part of the migrated people -- people who migrated to the West were most of a young age, starting from 14 years old until 25 years old. Unfortunately, being faced with a new reality, with a completely new environment, which gives -- offers various possibilities. Unfortunately, most of them found it impossible to get integrated and they have chosen ways that destroyed, harmed the image, not only of their families but also of their country. If we see it from another viewpoint, let us imagine that these young people had constitutional care, had an education. Would they be involved in the road of crime? I'm convinced that there would have been very, very little. In a way, they were just left in the streets. Fate left them in the streets, and this is a good substance to get involved into crime. That is why there have been such cases in the western countries, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, which unfortunately, I have seen it with my own eyes in Switzerland. Some of my compatriots, I've seen what they have done. However, the majority, the overwhelming majority, is -- they have sacrificed -- made sacrifices, they've worked hard, even in doing hard jobs, just for the only goal of keeping their families in Kosovo. Because our hope was migration, and life in Kosovo during the time with millions unemployed, this hope had kept this overwhelming majority of people who migrated, just doing all kinds of jobs. I'm talking about honest jobs. But unfortunately, as I said, there were such who made the lives of those who did honest jobs very difficult. I'd like to talk about the Kosovo Liberation Army. Your Honours, as I mentioned before, under such a situation, at the time when no one sees you, when no one gives you even a single sign of hope that things will get better, that something will improve, that a kind of a prospect will be here, at the time when the violence was not -- was increasing, the occupation was increasing, then there comes the time for survival. Then you have to lay yourself against the wall and there is no other outcome; there's no solution. There comes what we call -- I cannot -- if I cannot do things for myself, then let the others do it. Or: What can I do for my own country which would help my -- which would help me and my country to overcome this situation I'm faced with? There are many questions like these that every person in Kosovo has asked such a question. And I've asked this question to myself many times, because I had a family to support. It is said that many people want to enjoy the life when they don't have it, and because that's why they want life more. I would like to say that I'm sure that life is not -- is no precious for the person who really wants to give this life for his own country. Because there are two ways: Either to live humiliated or to live free. And I'm proud of finding the road, the way, the best possible way, the road to freedom, for what I was able to do, for what I knew. And this is at best seen and appreciated by the citizens of Kosovo. Whatever words we say here, my work that I've done for my Kosovo, and Kosovo will praise my work, my activity, my engagement and my behaviour. This is vital to me. My involvement in the UCK, after the arrests that were carried out in 1997, which prompted me to leave Kosovo, and I'm going to talk shortly about this period and the fact that I lived one year in Switzerland, where I was granted the right to political asylum. And I'd like to thank the Swiss government and the people for granting me this possibility and have a care granted by the state. On the other hand, I'd like to say that I have tried, I did my best to obey, to respect the law of the hosting country, and I've respected that law. I worked there and I did jobs, just like the majority of Albanians did. I did all kinds of jobs. I was not selective. I didn't want to live from the social aid that I was granted. And I've seen that the Prosecution, and even the bills of my salaries, they included those in the exhibits, those that were included the period during the time in Switzerland. Because my entirely family was in Kosovo and I had to help my family there and I also was dealing with -- was engaged in activity with -- of -- carried out by the Albanian migrants in Kosovo -- in Switzerland. I tried to organise and help and collect financial resources for the Kosovo Liberation Army. I joined the people there who were dealing with their activities. And I think we've done a good job. The events of February 1998 -- I'm talking about the February events, the massacre of Likosane and which culminated with the massacre in Prekaz, at a time when Serbia did not save even children, women, old people; nothing. Serbia spared nothing and killed the legendary commander, Ademi Jashari and his brother, in an effort to protect his family. This was a clear signal to us and to all Albanians that Serbia had started to take other steps; that is, they were carrying out a massive elimination of Albanians. No order was given to me, either to join UCK or to return from Switzerland to Kosovo. Not only me, but I say it with full -- I bear full responsibility here, that no one, no one ordered anyone else to return from the West and come to Kosovo. This is something -- it's publicly known throughout Kosovo. I did it at my own will, or if I can call it a will, because it was not a real will, but as they had no other choice, they came back and joined the UCK ranks. Your Honours, it was said here yesterday that the Kosovo Liberation Army was structured, organised, separated into zones from May, February, April, and then July, August. It's such a short time. In one year -- sorry. It was organised in one year, has fought and got transformed. I would kindly ask you to have a different approach to the conflict in Kosovo and in Croatia, due to the short period of time and due to the nature of it. The Kosovo Liberation Army, when we returned to Kosovo, I would say that there were approximately 200 members in that army at that time. So it is -- it's about March 1998. At the time when it is about the month of May, period of time when they say that KLA was organised, was structured. The place where I stayed, place of Klecka, there were seven of us, seven soldiers. At that time, Your Honour, the KLA was nothing but a guerrilla. The developments after the murder of the legendary commander, Ademi Jashari, that it had in Kosovo had an impact in the soul of each and every Kosovar and that did mobilise every Kosovar. And for a short period of time, KLA grew up, because in the very beginning it was only a guerrilla group. These events demonstrated that general headquarters of the KLA wasn't very much prepared for the new events. If one could call it an infrastructure, then it would be a guerrilla infrastructure. And you could think of a structure with three people only working. So the duties were to attack the Serbian forces and then to retreat. According to what it is said later, it comes out that the leaders of the KLA were planning for years and years for the expansion of the KLA, but the events developed in a dramatic way. And we were facing a situation where the biggest optimists, be it locals or internationals, were not expecting any good developments during the spring of Kosovo. As I stated, from a guerrilla group, it started growing as a popular movement, at the time when the general headquarters absolutely lacked the infrastructure. No one was prepared for such a development. Then what should it do? Like to get armed or to start the organisation -- the structural organisation? Those thousands of people, for three months, were involved with the KLA around the flag. Students, villagers, intellectuals, citizens, young people, elder, females, males. And please bear in mind that all those people were members of LDK. Someone was trying to imply here that the LDK was against KLA. But it's a good thing that our people do not trust any longer to this insinuations. Citizens of Kosovo cannot -- from all of this mess, where people, with their own initiative, in their own villages, in their own neighbourhoods, were getting organised to defend themselves. As I stated, KLA appeared as a meteor. It was enough to say that we were members of KLA. Everyone joined the common interests. We were referred to as saviours. We were referred to as the hope, the solution. Everyone joined each other around the flag. And there are no proceedings to solutions like this. There is no infrastructure on these occasions. Everything was done on a voluntary basis at that time. And this expansion, and also the fact that the KLA was getting massive, was becoming massive, led to the expansion of KLA in different parts of Kosovo. After the offensive that took place in summer, the KLA wasn't a military organised organisation. And at that time, KLA operated in units in different villages. There was enough for ten people to carry weapons, and one of them would be led as the commander. When I say one of them would be appointed as commander, I would like to provide you with an example. One of the commanders was mentioned here yesterday. By the end of zone, in the operative zone of Drenica, in the zone of Drenica, that would be the main zone, operative zone of KLA, the oldest one, from the units that operated throughout the whole territory of Drenica, the commanders of the zone was elected by votes. And then that election was turned into an appointment by the general headquarters. This occurred in June, if I'm not mistaken. This would be the first organisation of KLA. And then other organisations followed. But that was interrupted by the summer offensive. I'm sorry that I do not have a map of the territory with me. There was a total displacement of my place of action, place of operation. I'm still stating, Your Honours, that the time factor is very important. In Kosovo and inside of KLA, things could take place in a night, which are things that could not take place in a professional army, because that was a totally voluntary organisation. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to take into consideration the factor, the time factor, because those were dramatic developments. I'm taking only an example. In May of 1999 -- 1998, we were only seven. At the place which I led, in the municipality of Malisevo, which has 53.000 inhabitants, there were 35 soldiers, approximately. In three months, the number of the armed soldiers in that municipality exceeded 2.000, whereas 5.000 or 6.000 others were expecting to get weapons. And this expectation would go like this: One would rest on the other, with substitute him, would take his weapon, and so on. So May 1998 and May 1999, the KLA at the same time had to fight, to get supplied, to get organised, to defend itself, and this only in one year. And in the end, to get transformed, in the end, after the KFOR entered Kosovo. It is not by accident the historian Judah represents this as the most great achievements of the modern history. As I stated, I don't have a map with me. What would the term "region" mean? What would one mean with the term "region"? This term, in the KLA and in Kosovo, is quite unknown. These terms are mentioned in the KLA. Units that have operated in villages or different points, two levels. General headquarters and then the unit. Then, by mid-June, we are dealing with the beginning of the formation of the zones. It started with the zone of Drenica, which then stopped, and then the zone of Pastrik and Dukagjin, and after the summer offensive we have the creation of the brigades and other companies. That process of the formation did not start even after the completion of the war, but at least the main goals were known. I think that when it comes to time to the matter when it will be about the statements, I would have a chance to give a more clear statement on this. The thing that you might have -- you should have into account, Your Honour, is the responsibility issue. For the time, we are speaking of, the time this indictment is relevant, each and every commander of the KLA can be held responsible for his point. There was no other area of responsibility. So this is the territory that has this commander, this territory that it is under their responsibility of this or that person. There were no such things at that time. Villages that were mentioned here were -- these are change of facts because it is about the period covering the end of August, when a brigade was founded which involved all units at that time, not as it was represented in the map that was shown yesterday. And from these units was created -- was founded a brigade, as instructed by the general headquarters. And I was appointed as the commander of this brigade. The tendency to represent such an organisation as something that occurred on April, May, or July is unstable [as interpreted]. Your Honour, I'm saying -- I'm repeating it time and again that from all of the things I have done until now throughout my life, I have no reasons to feel myself humiliated, to have a bad conscience, as we say. On the contrary; everything I've done until this moment is as clear as daylight. Without modesty, I have to say that not only in Kosovo but in the Balkans, and in other countries, if you look at the biography of someone, I don't think you'll find another that is clearer or purer than mine, because I have been transparent in everything I've done. Whatever I've done, it has been in the service of my country and in the service of all. I was an idealist. Sometimes even naive, I would say. Why do I say this? Because I dreamt of another Kosovo from the one that I saw after 1999, and I cannot say that I am content at what I've seen after 1999 and what I see now. I dreamt of a free Kosovo, a Kosovo that would be in the service of all its citizens, a Kosovo that would give opportunities to all, a Kosovo where its citizens would be proud at being its citizens. But unfortunately, this has not come true. My country is not what I dreamt of. It's a different country. But I hope that it will become as I want it to be. Your Honour, in the pre-trial brief, they spoke about the conflict. My aim was for me, in 1998, was a war. There was a war, irrespective of how that is seen in the context of international law, for me, in 1998, we had a war, and that was the case also for all the people in my country. I don't want to discuss it, whether it was a conflict or not, but I want to come back to what the Prosecutor said yesterday. It's interesting to note that when it's a question of speaking about something that is beneficial for Kosovo, nobody says anything about it. It's not respected; it's not appreciated. When it comes to harming it or accusing it, then millions of documents are produced to accuse its war. I'm giving you an example. Maybe it would be important for you to bear in mind that in no way, when we talk about Serbian-perpetrated crimes, the aim is not to justify them. I am aware of the crimes perpetrated, isolated instances of crimes or murders. Such things may have happened. But I am saying that if we say why the Serbs are not accused for their acts, this is not that we want to justify what has happened with us. As you heard yesterday, the Prosecutor said that in 1998 there was a conflict in Kosovo because Serbian police and army killed children and women in Kosovo. Then, later, it said for the crimes committed in Kosovo we have two indictments. But the names of the people, I'm saying there are two indictments. One indictment is against Mr. Milosevic for crimes in Kosovo, Bosnia, and Croatia, and other one for Kosovo with seven or six persons. Then it says for the crimes committed by the Serbian forces in Kosovo in January to June 1999. They forget what happened in 1998. Again I'm saying -- I don't want to justify anything, just to draw your attention to this fact, what did happen in reality or what is happening now. Your Honour, from February 1998 to December, according to incomplete data by non-government organisations in Kosovo, about 3.000 civilians have been killed and wounded. Among them, 500 children and women, aging three months old to 14 years. Many women were pregnant. In 1998, I want to remind you of some of the massive crimes, massacres, committed in Kosovo which are public knowledge. I think this is a good chance to mention them. During this year, these massacres were perpetrated: Qerez massacre, Likosane massacre, Prekaz massacre, Poklek massacre, Obrinje massacre, Ljubenic massacre, Golubovac massacres, and other massacres. Allow me to, in a few words, to single out the massacre in Obrinje, for one single reason: Because it had a political impact or implications after that. I want to thank outstanding British journalist. He has made public this fact, this massacre. If I'm not wrong -- if I am wrong, I apologise to the BBC reporter, whose name I don't remember. He makes known the massacre that is known in Kosovo by the name of massacre of Deliu family. Because that journalist was capable of shooting the victims and broadcasting those views that shocked the entire public opinion, which led to the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke. This is an example to show what horrors were perpetrated in Kosovo in 1998 and for which the Prosecutor has been indifferent. The failure to institute proceedings for any of these massacres or murders of those 3.000 people or failure to make any indictments for these crimes committed in 1998 cannot be explained otherwise than with the fact that the Prosecutor has closed both eyes and has overlooked these crimes committed in 1998 and forgiving the Serbian forces for all the crimes committed. On the other hand, they tried by all costs to criminalise KLA for these three months period given the situation we were in not being sufficient and content with the fact that with the number of Serbs committed by counting the Serbs killed all over the places, beginning from Belgrade and in the border and everywhere. In Lapusnik, the border of Belgrade to Lapusnik is 200 kilometres long. So anything might happen. So as far as I know, about 100 Serbs were killed or disappeared in 1998. I don't want to make a distinction between the numbers, because victims are victims. They are all the same. Not only the victims of my country, of my people, but everywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I want to express my condolences to the victims, because they are victims, victims of a genocide committed against my family, my people. I know what it means to suffer victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but our tapes are about to reach their end, so we must break now. We will break. Could I invite you to give consideration to when you will be concluding your statement, because you will understand another person is to follow you today. We will adjourn now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Limaj. THE ACCUSED LIMAJ: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to thank you very much for your patience and the possibility you granting me to offer this short overview. I will continue where I left. Please allow me to first of all thank my family, then my neighbourhood, the place where I was born, the town where I was born, my country, my professors, the political leaders and intellectual leaders of my country who undoubtedly have the great -- should be given the greatest credit of making me the human being, that person that I am today. Thanks to their education given to me, I'm proud of my actions, I'm proud of my life, I'm proud of everything I've done so far, because this has been a human education, very humane, and, above all, an education that has always inspired me to determine my own way in life. Your Honour, one of the strata that is most respected in the world are those activists who fight for the protection of human rights, in various non-governmental organisations, being in the government, not -- it has not very seldom happened that those whose rights were being violated in a drastic way had been condemned or punished just because they protected the rights of their own people. They were punished and sentenced with years and years in the name of justice. I'd like to remind you and mention here two occasions -- three, three, sorry. In the long run, sees the creation of the world or our era, as we might say, was the Christ crucified and did it plunder. Then I would mention two other occasions, honourable well-known world personality figure Nelson Mandela. For years and years on end he stood in prisons in the name of justice. He stayed, and at the end, the South African people won their rights, while the world won racial equality. Fortunately, and I say -- I'm very proud of saying this here, I belong to a people who, among many dignitaries and those people who have granted to the humanity, and that small people, that small nation, has also rendered a contribution to humanity. This small people has given Mother Teresa to this humanity. This small people with its works has served to the mankind and has given another hero, Judge Kastri Skanderbevo [phoen]. At the same time, I'm proud belonging, being part of this people, who even in the new era has given not only to Kosovo, has given an example also to Kosovo and Europe as how to protect human rights. And this was Adem Demaqi, a symbol of resistance or, as it is well known, as Mandela of Europe, and he has received the Saharov prize. Allow me just to say one of his sayings here. The broader the freedom is, the greater and broader the care towards minority communities, toward other ethnic communities, the broader our freedom will be. This saying that leads -- that most of the Kosovar people are led nowadays, despite news coming from Kosovo, but please believe that this is one of the sayings that most of the people are led by today, by this postulate, and the way our institutions work there today. As I said earlier today, this kind of strata is being praised for their protection of human rights because they are engaged in many countries of the crisis, in the areas of crisis, regardless of their ethnic pertainence [as interpreted], or nationality. They go there and help the people and they publish human rights abuses. However, I'd like to ask you, Your Honour: Is there a greater engagement to protect the rights of a people than readiness to give your own life for the rights to protect the rights of these people, than the readiness that a 25-year-old man - and when I say 25-year-old, I'm not talking about myself, but about thousands and thousands of my compatriots - who are ready to sacrifice their own selves just to protect the rights of this people, of this country. I'm proud of mentioning the dignitaries I said before and I'm proud of my country, who has given me that education. And as a result of this upbringing and education, we always were able to distinguish, to make a distinction what is the Serbian people and what is a criminal regime. And under the spirit, we have seen the criminal regime as something terrible, something -- as something evil that is also for Serbia itself and the Serbian people who, unfortunately, were -- the Serbian people who were represented by this regime. The KLA, willy-nilly, and this is a historic fact, is a promotor of the positive changes that happened in the region, in that area, and in that area that has suffered for a long time. Why? Because it was facing the KLA, went to the forefront to protect human values, civilised values. And as a result of protecting those values which were endangered, which were entirely endangered, for years on end, and now they were facing a complete elimination. The KLA went up to the aid and action of NATO in Kosovo. The Western world could not allow those democratic values and that kind of civilisation in Europe to be endangered and to be -- to expand further. That is why, as I've stated, everywhere, even Kosovo, because the Balkan mentality very often, if someone -- if you give someone a support, they think that you're against the other. I just wanted that my own people does not fall prey of such indications. And I've said this in public, everywhere, whenever I was given the indication, that NATO did not come to Kosovo because they love Albanians or because they are against the Serbs. NATO came to Kosovo to protect democratic values and civilised values that were on the verge of destruction. And for NATO, everyone is the same. Honourable Judges, what I said earlier here about what happened in 1998, it is not a price, it is not that the victims in Kosovo are being ignored. To ignore 3.000 victims and among those I'm including the 20 victims that I am accused of here, because never -- I will never, never accept that I was involved with their fate. It is not saying -- being ignored that no one bears responsibility for such crimes, but to try by all means to raise an indictment against the KLA, the Prosecutor, facing lack of facts that has taken from the Serbian security service and the criminal regime of Milosevic, would like to put Albanians, to involve Albanians into a game here, to satisfy the standards of an indictment. As Albanians allegedly were endangered, that it is not enough number of Serbs, so let us concoct an indictment against the KLA. It was said here that this is a good example to unite the two peoples together. In this way, this way does not only connect or serve the two peoples or serve to the peace, but it leaves room for tendency that within my own people, this might cause reactions. Anyway, in any case, I would like to say, Your Honour, in front of you here and in front of all of us, we will hear various witnesses here, Serb witnesses. I'd like to mention one occasion that I've heard at this trial, at this Tribunal, that one person which is providing his evidence as a witness of the Prosecution, describing the situation in Kosovo in 1998, 1999, says the following: I was in Krusa. It's a small village in Kosovo. We say Big Krusa and Small Krusa. These are two villages that many, many massacres have taken place. All the men of those villages were killed. Terrible massacres were committed in these villages and their family members are found in the bridges of Belgrade, in the backyards of the secret police, into the refrigerators of someone, and no one is interested to know where these people are. He says the following: "When I entered the village, instead of air, I was breathing the stench of blood." Why I'm saying this to you? Because here, after a few days, a witness from the Prosecution will be the commander of the Serbian forces who had led those massacres in those places. Now he comes again here to judge and to provide evidence against victims here. And he will be a witness against us. Everyone here, let us recall to your conscience and see where this is leading us to or is the crime that is being judged or the victim? Is it worth -- is it worth doing this for career or for various interests to come up to this level? My fate, my personal fate, is of concern to me, to tell you the truth, because I've given my fate once for Kosovo and because if God has foreseen my fate to be as such, I'm ready to accept this fate. It's no problem at all. I'm not concerned at all. I feel sorry for the international justice. This is -- it's my opinion for the international justice, what I think of it, and this has been an ideal opinion of mine before. I'm sorry for my people, because much is being played with these people, with my own people. Your Honour, my country whom I belong is used to injustice, just as it is known that United Kingdom is known as the cradle of democracy, or let's say western Europe is known as such. Just as a British man in the first view might know -- might realise whether a country is democratic or not, having a long tradition, unfortunately, we -- if I can call it a favour, but it is not a favour, no one in Europe, I believe no country, no people, no nation in Europe would be able to see the injustice before we, the Albanians, do so. Because we have lived in injustice for a long period of time. I would like to say one more thing. The Yugoslav system started to be destroyed in Kosovo because of injustices or a system, a legal system that was completely, entirely against Albanians. Today, as long as in Croatia and Bosnia, those who fought for their own country are being respected and honoured and a place to live is being ensured to them, to live with their own family. Their integration is provided for these people, other facilities to find is a job. In my country, the contrary is taking place. In my country, UNMIK has found -- has chosen the shortest and less expensive way. For the majority of the KLA members, they are getting -- the majority of the KLA members, they are getting the former prisons as a reward. About 500 members of the KLA so far had gone through the institutions of the so-called transparent justice. Hundreds were held in detention for a long time, with no kind of explanation at all, no other judgement or no indictment raised against them. Dozens of them were punished and they're serving their gaol terms. Some of them have condemned for war crimes. I want to draw the attention of the Prosecutors that the methods that they want to use, to resort to in the Hague Tribunal have been already utilised in Kosovo and the Kosovo people no longer trust such matters. Your Honour, I'm saying here too what it means not to have a state. We are -- we feel here like orphans. For 20 months, the treatment we have received has been quite different from that of other inmates. Nobody is allowed from the official bodies is allowed to come and visit us. UNMIK doesn't care at all about us. Our own institutions allege lack of competences, of powers; I don't know what. So, in real terms, in the absence of an institutional care, we feel here -- we are in your hands. I feel as if we are abandoned. Nobody can draw the -- can reprimand those who violate our rights. We are the only ones submitted to such treatment so far, I think. Every state has its representatives, can establish links. Every group of prisoners from the former republics of Yugoslavia have, under the law, care ensured to their family, to themselves, they receive various financial and legal assistance. Whereas in our case, nobody cares. Nobody has done anything, despite the initiatives taken by some local institutions, they have been thwarted. I think it's high time that we began to be treated differently. I think we deserve a human treatment. I hope that those institutions there will see what is really happening with its citizens, because before everything, we are Kosovar citizens and we are here, and efforts are being made to write the new history of Kosovo according to the instructions of the Prosecutor's office. Your Honour, I'm about to conclude, but there is one thing I want to say. In the absence of this institutional care, despite this horrible situation we are in, despite the injustices committed against us, despite the constant threats made to our family, I want to make it known to you: Our families in Kosovo are constantly subjected to pressure and threats. We have the support of the people of the citizens of Kosovo, of those for whom we fought, and they are helping us in all possible ways. And this keeps us going. Every citizen in Kosovo has, in his own way, shown his support, her support, through written letters, through open expressions of sympathy, and this is what keeps us going, as I said. Our families have been -- are constantly subjected to pressure. Kosovo is led by UNMIK, and the security issue is its prerogative. You may bring all Kosovo here if you want. Every single member of -- former member of Kosovo Liberation Army you can bring here. If you can't bring here the real culprits, you can bring just an ordinary citizen or ordinary member. You can even imprison my own mother. Because, of course she will curse, curse people for bringing me here. And you can accuse her. You can levy any accusation against her. I feel threatened. We are threatened. In the last month, the pressures have been great. Without any warning, we have been banned to communicate with our families, with our country, for any reason at all. The detention officer who has told us -- he has said that we have never violated any rules, any rules in the pre-detention cells. And for no reason at all, as I said, they are not allowed to visit us, and this happens only in the case of the Albanians of Kosovo because people think that they can do anything with us because there is no one to take care of them, no one to look after them. Another thing: I hope, Your Honour, and I'm convinced that justice that will be meted out in this Tribunal in your judgement, but until now I want to say things have been going on according to the old Chinese saying: "When there is a will to punish, to condemn someone, the evidence is found." Or, as Hilary Clinton says in her book of memories, when she describes a well-known American lawyer, she says: "If the prosecutors come into play, they can indict -- can build indictments even for a sandwich." I think that Chinese saying I mentioned, I'm afraid is being the rationale of what's happening here, at least from what we heard yesterday. Allow me now to say -- to refer to a saying of a French lady whom I think suits my situation now and our situation. After the Second World War, a French lady whose name was Michelle Morelle said in the first hours after she was freed, after the capitulation of fascism, she says: "In the early morning of freedom, distrustful of the reality," she says, "I was in ecstasy, paralysing ecstasy. I was trying to tell myself that I was free. I tried," she said, "to write a poem, but I never managed to say more than I'm free, I'm free, and finally free." She said: "For me, so far the concept of freedom was not broader than that." Your Honour, by mention of this, I want to say that for as long as the concept of freedom was not broader than me for this French lady and for the French after the Second World War, unfortunately for my people too, even though five years have passed, this concept has not become broader; it's shrinking, in fact. It's being poisoned, undermined. I hope that those who have the obligations to do things will come to realise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the long-suffering people is not content only with having freedom and not being beaten, but freedom has a broader meaning, to be able to determine your own fate, to be able to find a job, to work, and to live as you wish. Yesterday, the Prosecutor explained their views about what a criminal I was, with exception of the fact that if I had been a Serb army officer, then everything would be okay. I'm saying -- I mean those officers who have done bad things, not professional ones. Your Honour, I'm proud, and thank God for enabling me that together with my co-fighters, I can defend about 85.000 civilians who were constantly, for six months, endangered by special units, Serbian units, led by a notorious criminal who is being tried today in Serbia, Miodrag Lukovic, Legija. And you can imagine what a man he is who, having no more to kill, killed his own prime minister. So this is where -- this is how we should see Lapusnik. He was leader of the operations in Lapusnik. I hope that time will clarify everything. Members of the Serbian secret service will testify, those who for years have constructed, orchestrated, executed the policy of extermination of my own nation. After all, Serbia itself is facing the remnants of that regime and of that service. Kindly look at the Belgrade officials and look what this secret service constitutes for Serbia itself. Imagine what it did for Kosovo and what it does. Those remnants have blackmailed and are blackmailing people in Kosovo too, in order to do the same thing. Someone wishes that the Serbian UDBA makes Albanians condemn not Fatmir Limaj but Kosovo. I'm certain that they will fail in their goal, because now we are free and we know what freedom means. The freedom that Kosovo has today, distinguished gentlemen, Honours, is not a freedom that I brought from my family. Those hands which yesterday were described as bloody hands, in those hands, and many hands of my co-fighters today, we have -- we keep the smiles of our children. Now we have creches, kindergartens, schools open. Life is going on. Children are smiling. Their parents are no longer scared for the fate of their kids. And I am happy, indeed, that even if I did something, little as it might be, I did it for my country. I contributed to my country, even though it cost me my imprisonment. And I cannot enjoy the freedom I worked for and that the Prosecutor's office has, for the moment, banned my dreams and separated me from my love. The only thing that I know is that if I were in Kosovo today, when in that country there is need also for my contribution to help build that democratic society, this saddens me and makes me suffer, because I have no possibilities to contribute to the building of the democratic society which was the ideal for all the citizens of Kosovo. But I hope that I will have the possibilities to go back and render my contribution to where it's most needed and to where I can. Finally, it's an old saying of my people which goes: Suspicion is like the fog that covers, the mist that covers the beautiful landscape. This fog which has been -- the Prosecutor's office has been constantly trying to create -- to cover -- with which to cover my personality. I hope, Your Honours, you will be able to dispel, in order to look at the true picture lying behind it, look at my true personality and realise who I am, who I was, and whether I deserve to be where I am today. Your Honours, I wish that we are no longer subjected to the same treatment we've been subjected so far, but be treated in the way we deserve. We don't want more or less than the other inmates. Also, I want -- I'd like to say that the positive atmosphere prevailing, the support I have in the Kosovo people, which the Prosecutor's office looks upon with jealousy, I want this -- and wishes deliberately to transform into a threatening atmosphere for its witnesses, I'm not, Your Honour, guilty of enjoying the respect of each and every family in Kosovo. Your Honour, I am not to blame because in every respect the people of Kosovo have shown their support for me and appreciate my work and activity. In Kosovo, there is no sympathy -- I mean, there is no hatred against the Hague Tribunal. The sympathy for me does not mean that the people there are against the Tribunal. You can see that for yourselves. The people say that they trust the Tribunal, but at the same time they trust me, and I don't see anything wrong in this. There is no negative tendency there as to what's going on here. It only demonstrates that this people has seen in this court a window to their hopes, because they are victims. They think that here the criminals who have wreaked havoc in Kosovo are going to be tried. For them, the only hope that for the first time in our history the true criminals are going to be punished and condemned which unfortunately is not the case. The opposite is happening. Some suspicions arise as if Albanians are being used as scapegoats, as cards, as a means to make up to the others just because Belgrade wants it, whether there are facts or not. We have to make an indictment by all means. You can, as I said earlier, you can arrest and bring here as many people as you want from Kosovo but you have to be worried about the credibility of what's going on here and especially how much the process is being undermined in Kosovo and in international justice. Thanking you for your passions, for the possibility you gave me to express my views, to make this statement. Your Honour, again, in conclusion, I want to express my regret and condolences to all the victims, be them from my people or the Serbian people. I hope that the true culprits, all the tragedy incurred, will be found and condemned. Because as it is -- because the victims will be condemned only if you -- only if you condemn the true culprits. They want the murderers, the assassins, those who have caused them pain. In front of you is not the assassin, the killer of the victims but the defender of the victims who has tried to serve his people as much as he has to bring his country, his freedom, and I am happy for what I have done in the service of my country. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Limaj. Mr. Guy-Smith, it is the position, I understand, that the Defence of Mr. Bala prefers to -- not to make a statement at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct. We will be reserving that right until a later point in time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Now, Mr. Topolski, I'm sorry. I think we each may have thought that you would have been able to speak today, but we must break at a quarter to to enable the court to be readied for 2.15 for the next. So it will be tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Courtesy of you to apologise, but what we've just heard, of course, is important, and I shall be ready to proceed tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will adjourn now until 2.15 tomorrow. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to delay you for one minute only, and that is out of courtesy to the Tribunal, I wanted to indicate that owing to commitments in London that have been running all this year, it's one matter, it's about to conclude, I do have to return there for a day or two. I have liaised with my co-counsel and matters that are certainly -- we have an interest in will be covered by others. But I felt it rather than just not be here, that you should know that it's a professional engagement, I'm afraid, which has been going on for nine months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Mansfield. I'm sure that Mr. Khan will be ready and willing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I raise one matter before we adjourn? Because I see Mr. Mansfield is not going to be here tomorrow. Our next witness, Ole Lehtinen, is the investigating officer on the case. I've raised the matter with Mr. Topolski. We'd like to be able to speak with him about matters not connected with his testimony after he's sworn, because he is the investigating officer on the case and we need him for other purposes. And I would just like to secure the Court's permission on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. Do you mean during his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During his evidence we may need to speak to him about matters not connected with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long would you expect him to be giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Two to three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see. Well, I will turn to those on the other side. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it's a little difficult to respond, since it's in somewhat circuitous terms. Obviously I accept everything Mr. Cayley says; I'm not suggesting anything else. But it's a little difficult for us to say. It's an unusual practice, and he's not saying that it's unconnected with the case, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If it is connected with the case, if it's possible to give us some idea of what it is that is so important that can only be dealt with as he goes through it, it would help us make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he being the investigating officer on the case, assists us with getting witnesses here and we need him for that purpose. Now, if we can't deal with him, then we can't bring witnesses in to follow his evidence. So that's what we would need to talk to him about, not matters connected to his testimony or evidence in the case, simply securing the presence of witnesses here. And that's what we need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Mansfield, is there any objection to Mr. Cayley speaking about the movement of other witnesses to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, obviously there wouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just add that if it's possible for someone else to do that, a unit that's concerned with it, then I'd ask, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understanding that the discussions will be limited to the matters raised, I have no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It was that which Mr. Cayley indicated me would be the sole and only purpose of any communication with a witness under oath, and it was upon that basis I indicated my agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I still do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On that limited and explicit basis, Mr. Cayley, yes, you may communicate with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The adjournment will now occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
